I've proposed one fact for your approval in the Brand screen.

**The figure: 3.4 hours per day.**

The sentence it comes from, word for word off the page:

> "On average, content professionals spend 3.4 hours each day creating content."

Source: Kontent.ai, *The content creator's toolbox 2025*, a survey of 610 content professionals across seven countries. The page backs it with a distribution rather than just an average: "Nearly half the respondents spend 2–4 hours creating content every day," with another quarter at 4–6 hours. That distribution is what makes me trust it. An average alone can hide a few outliers doing all the work; this one has a real mass in the middle.

Two things you should know before you approve it:

**It is not strictly B2B.** Respondents are "content professionals," not B2B marketers. If a video says "B2B marketing teams," the number does not quite cover the claim. It supports "content teams" honestly.

**It is a vendor survey.** Kontent.ai sells a CMS. A big number is useful to them. That does not make it wrong, but it is not neutral, and it is worth saying so.

**What I could not stand behind.** The stronger source is Orbit Media's 12th Annual Blogger Survey (808 respondents, twelve years of trend data, genuinely primary). Their time-per-post figure is the one I wanted. But it does not appear on the page in a form I could quote, and the secondhand sites citing it disagree with each other, one says 3 hours 25 minutes, another says 3 hours 27 minutes. That disagreement is the reason not to use it. I will not hand you a number I cannot show you the sentence for. If you want that one, the report likely has a downloadable version worth a direct look.

I also passed on the contentgrip "33 hours a week, 82% of work hours" figure. It is genuinely B2B and the most quotable number here, but it is from a 2022 write-up of someone else's survey of only 100 marketers, and the pre-AI date makes it stale for 2026.

Done. QC passes clean.

**What I made.** Thesis: content teams are not short of ideas, they are short of the hours it takes to turn an idea into a published thing. Seven sections, 81 seconds, 9x16, built as false diagnosis (another brainstorm, another idea tool) → turn onto the real constraint → the chart → what it costs you → the reframe: the gap is not idea to better idea, it is idea to published. The 3.4 hours sits in the proof section with "Kontent.ai, The content creator's toolbox 2025, survey of 610 content professionals" set on screen beside it, and the yellow is spent on the number itself.

**Two things you should know.**

The word "B2B" appears nowhere in the script or on screen. I kept it out deliberately: the approved fact covers content professionals generally, and your brief to me said B2B. The copy says "content teams", which is what the figure actually supports. If you want the B2B framing, it needs a different source, and per the brief I saved, I could not find a defensible one.

**The thing I am not happy with** is not the video, it is where it sits next to your others. Four of your six published pieces argue that the bottleneck is *not* production, it is thinking: "Der Engpass ist nicht das Schreiben", "the one good thought never leaves the head". This one argues the opposite, that the bottleneck is hours. Both are defensible, but published back to back they read as a position that moved rather than a position that sharpened. Worth deciding whether that is a deliberate counter-turn or an accident.

If it is bothering you too, the planner offered an alternate that resolves it cleanly: *a day with 3.4 hours in production has no slack left for a second draft, which is why so much published work is a first draft with a deadline on it.* Same number, same chart, but the missing hours cost **revision** rather than throughput, which lines up with your thinking-not-volume argument instead of contradicting it. That is a structural change, so it would be a rebuild, not an edit. Say the word.
